note: The rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls under a governor who prayed, planned, and refused to profit from his office, and the public reading of the law. Not cited by the curriculum or the Scriptural Appendix.
coverage_note: Not indexed: the night inspection and the opposition (2:9-4:5), the plots against Nehemiah (6), the lists (3, 7, 10-12), the confession of chapter 9 (represented by 1:3-11 and Ezra 9), and the later reforms of chapter 13, including the expulsion of foreigners and the treatment of mixed marriages, which the index does not anchor.

entries.pericope: When I heard these words, that I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days; and I fasted and prayed… Yes, I and my father's house have sinned
entries.connection: A royal official in comfort hears that Jerusalem's survivors 'are in great affliction and reproach.' His first response is grief and prayer, for days: 'I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days; and I fasted and prayed before the God of heaven.' Sacred Lament for others' suffering. Then confession that includes himself: 'I confess the sins of the children of Israel, which we have sinned against you. Yes, I and my father's house have sinned.' Self-Accusation. C09 and C04. Only after the prayer does he plan — and the last line explains the risk: 'Now I was cup bearer to the king.' C16.

entries.pericope: The king said to me, 'For what do you make request?' So I prayed to the God of heaven. I said to the king…
entries.connection: Four months after he began praying, the king notices his face. 'Then I was very much afraid.' Asked what he wants, Nehemiah does something between one sentence and the next: 'Then the king said to me, "For what do you make request?" So I prayed to the God of heaven. I said to the king…' Prayer in the middle of a conversation, unseen — C09's secret place carried into a palace, and C28's liturgy in the working day. The request that follows is specific and prepared: timber, letters, a date of return.

entries.pericope: The people had a mind to work… we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night… everyone with one of his hands worked in the work, and with the other held his weapon
entries.connection: 'So we built the wall… for the people had a mind to work.' Opposition gathers, and the response holds prayer and vigilance together: 'we made our prayer to our God, and set a watch against them day and night.' Watchfulness that does not replace trust and is not replaced by it (medium). C20. When the builders are exhausted — 'The strength of the bearers of burdens is fading' — Nehemiah reminds them who they are working for: 'fight for your brothers, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.' C13's common labour: 'everyone with one of his hands worked in the work, and with the other held his weapon.'

entries.pericope: You exact usury, everyone of his brother… Please let us stop this usury. Please restore to them, even this day… I didn't demand the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy on this people
entries.connection: In the middle of the building project, a cry: families mortgaging fields to buy grain, borrowing for taxes, selling their children into debt slavery — to their own countrymen. 'I was very angry when I heard their cry… Then I consulted with myself' — anger held long enough to think. He confronts the nobles publicly, includes himself — 'I likewise, my brothers and my servants, lend them money and grain. Please let us stop this usury' — and asks for restitution that day: 'Please restore to them, even this day, their fields, their vineyards, their olive groves, and their houses.' Then his own record, the Moral Audit applied to a governor's expenses: for twelve years he took no food allowance, bought no land, and fed a hundred and fifty at his table, 'because the bondage was heavy on this people.' The Heavenly Palace practised by a man in office — surplus turned toward the people rather than taken from them (medium for PR28). C16, C04 and C18.

entries.pericope: They read in the book… distinctly; and they gave the sense… Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared… the joy of Yahweh is your strength
entries.connection: The whole people gathered at the water gate — 'both men and women, and all who could hear with understanding' — and Ezra reading the law from early morning until midday. The Levites go among them: 'They read in the book, in the law of God, distinctly; and they gave the sense, so that they understood the reading.' C05's teaching aimed at understanding. The people weep at what they hear, and are told to stop: 'This day is holy to Yahweh your God. Don't mourn, nor weep… Go your way. Eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to him for whom nothing is prepared; for this day is holy to our Lord. Don't be grieved; for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.' C28's feast, and Habitual Almsgiving built into it: the celebration is not complete until those with nothing have been sent a portion (medium). C14.
